rv.q: Even this year’s musical Pride , which explores similar themes and owes some of its DNA to Rent , feels less striking, less urgent. It works, then, that Luke Sheppard’s production opts to reiterate more than reimagine, in everything down to the costumes (designed by Gabriella Slade, they have that familiar shabby, chic Rent look).

But marking the show’s 30th anniversary (and returning to the former Duke of York’s, which hosted a reviled “updated” version in 2007), this rousing, faithful revival by Paddington director Luke Sheppard more than earns its keep. It boasts a strong West End debut, too, for Gaten Matarazzo.

It’s the story of La Bohème, kinda – taking a friendship circle of artists and wannabes from meet-cute in a power cut to last-act misery, riffing off Puccini’s sob-stringed melodies. Romances flare and falter, ambitions compromise, Aids is an ever-present anxiety.

Three decades on, his musical feels like something of a time capsule. There’s a fierce, sincere anger in the book and lyrics at the heartless gentrification of New York (now pretty much complete) and power in its centring of queer characters. But its earnestness, however on the money, feels heavy-handed.
We would recommend seeking this out for a great production of a classic musical which has clearly influenced Lin Manuel-Miranda while reminding how Jonathan Larson could have been the next Sondheim.

cn.t: Critics find this revival of the groundbreaking musical compelling, with Matarazzo perfectly cast as Mark. The show's portrayal of bohemian life in late '80s/early '90s New York continues to resonate with audiences.
